editorialConnections.recordTitle: Publication of Sefer Łuków by former residents in Israel and the United States

enrichment.markdown:
**Łuków Jewish community.** Outside sources place Łuków within the historical Lublin Jewish region, while also confirming its wider Podlasie connections. The community may have originated as early as the thirteenth century, but a substantial, organized kehilla existed by the sixteenth century. Its authority extended over as many as 163 surrounding towns and villages, making Łuków a regional religious and economic center. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/99-history/137635-history-of-community?utm_source=openai))

The JewishGen town file adds important name variants for future genealogy: **Likova, Lukov, Likeva, Likeve, and Lukova**. It records approximately 4,799 Jews in 1900 and preserves links to the 1968 *Sefer Łuków*, JRI-Poland, and related cemetery research. ([cdp.jewishgen.org](https://cdp.jewishgen.org/eastern-europe/poland/lukow?utm_source=openai))

**Sefer Łuków and the landsmanschaft.** JewishGen confirms that the memorial book was published in Tel Aviv in 1968 by former Łuków residents in Israel and the United States, edited by B. Heller. It also hosts a translation and a necrology supplied by Yad Vashem. This substantiates the organizational connection to the Łuków Jews in Israel, the American Łuków landsmanschaft, and Tel Aviv, although the sources located here do not provide a membership list or biographies of the editors. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/lukow.html?utm_source=openai))

**Synagogue and religious institutions.** The community possessed a Great Synagogue, several batei midrash, mikvaot, and prayer houses. A nineteenth-century prayer house on Browarna Street survived the war but was rebuilt afterward; the New Beit Midrash on Bożnicza Street, dating before 1792, was destroyed in the 1944 bombardment. The synagogue, beit midrash, and mikveh were concentrated around Trzebieska and Staropijarska Streets. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/112-synagogues-houses-of-prayer-and-others?utm_source=openai))

JewishGen’s translated memoirs add a religious connection absent from the record’s summary: Łuków had followers of Gur, Kotzk, Radzyń, and other Hasidic courts. Rabbi Hershel Morgenstern is described as the son of the Kotzker rabbi; his son, Rabbi Mendel Morgenstern, later served in Włodawa and was murdered with children sent to Sobibor. This supports the book’s association with the Kotzker Rebbe, but does not establish that every Łuków reference to “Kotzker” concerns the Rebbe personally. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/luk070.html?utm_source=openai))

**Cemetery.** The old cemetery was established around the 1750s near the Krzna River, while a newer cemetery was created in the nineteenth century on Warszawska Street. The old site was devastated during the occupation and later absorbed into hospital grounds; no visible graves remain. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/pl/miejscowosci/l/729-lukow/114-cmentarze/20585-cmentarz-zydowski-w-lukowie-ul-rogalinskiego?utm_source=openai))

**Persecution, ghetto, and mass killings.** The Łuków ghetto was established in May 1941 across several streets, including Browarna, Międzyrzecka, Kanałowa, Zdanowskiego, and Staropijarska. Deportations to Treblinka occurred in October 1942 and May 2, 1943; the latter transport removed roughly 2,000–3,000 people. The sources also describe killings inside the ghetto and the forced incorporation of Jews from nearby communities including Adamów, Kock, Radzyń-area villages, and Trzebieszów. ([sztetl.org.pl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/116-sites-of-martyrdom/48334-getto-w-lukowie?utm_source=openai))

No reliable outside archival matches were located here for **Aaron Nota Freiberg, Anshel Wamp, Berl Idls, Moshe Yaklen, Moshe Lichtenstein, or Hersh Leizer Lander** as individually documented persons. Searches used Łuków/Lukow/Lukov/Likova and variant forms across JewishGen, Yad Vashem, Virtual Shtetl, and USHMM-indexed material; the available results were community-level rather than securely person-specific.
